postText:
所有技术栈也都让 opus5.5 自己列出来！

Remotion 负责画面，Python 负责配乐，最后由 Remotion 调 ffmpeg 合成成片。

画面
影片工程是 Remotion 4.0.528，这是一个用 React 写视频的框架。每个镜头都是代码写的：截图摄影机的推拉和平移、案例标签、字幕、鼠标指针、点击反馈、片尾品牌卡。两个画幅共用同一份代码和同一条节拍时间轴，只是镜头参数不同。最后由 Remotion 调用 ffmpeg 编码成 H.264 的 mp4。

素材来源

网站截图：用 Playwright 在线上 http://goodcase.ai 实拍，桌面版 2 倍像素，手机版 3 倍像素。同时记下搜索框、案例卡、复制按钮这些元素的真实坐标，镜头才能准确推到它们上面。已复制 ✓ 那个状态，是给浏览器授了剪贴板权限后真的点了一下拍到的。
前期摸底：用 gstack 的无头浏览器看首页、读页面文字。
案例视频和图片：通过 http://goodcase.ai 的公开 API 查到媒体地址，用 curl 直接下载原文件，没有二次生成。

配乐
用 Python 配 numpy 和 scipy 从零合成，底鼓、拍手、踩镲、贝斯、拨弦、铺底、上升和下行扫频都是算出来的，再加上侧链和卷积混响。依赖用 uv 临时拉取，没有装进系统。混音检查靠 ffmpeg 的 ebur128 响度测量、频谱图和波形图。

质检
每一版都先渲染半分辨率小样，用 ffmpeg 抽关键帧拼成联络表逐场检查，改完再出正式版。最后用网站自己的 ESLint 和 tsc 确认新目录不影响网站构建。

至于模型：选素材、写分镜、写所有代码、调镜头都是我（Claude Opus 5.5）直接做的。整个过程没有调用任何 AI 视频或 AI 音乐生成服务。

postText:
Opus 5.5 is cracked at making animation.

I gave it a hand-drawn reference image and this prompt:

"Render a recipe motion graphic animation using JavaScript or HTML (whatever you think will produce the best result) to show the full recipe for a White Russian from start to finish, empty glass to completed cocktail. Explainer video style, showing the ingredients and measurements as they go into the glass. It should be a 30s video."

About 25 minutes later I had a finished 1080p MP4. One prompt, no follow-ups.

It built the whole thing as a single HTML file, using SVG and plain JavaScript with no animation library. Every frame is drawn from a timestamp, so it stepped a headless browser through all 900 frames and piped them straight into ffmpeg.

It got the physics right as well. The ice floats once the liquid reaches it, the coffee liqueur sinks and darkens the drink from the bottom, and the cream sits on top. I didn't tell it any of that.

Then it rendered test frames, found 3 problems and fixed them before exporting. Nobody asked it to check its own work.

This used to be a job for a motion designer and After Effects. 

Now it's one prompt.

What would you get it to animate next?

author: RaphaelAubryy
title: Ask me for: the product name and a one-line promise, 3 to 5 UI moments to…
prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for: the product name and a one-line promise, 3 to 5 UI moments to show, one accent color, 10 to 20 real vertical clips I own, and a royalty-free song with a clear drop (e.g. Mixkit, free for commercial use).
</inputs>

<direction>
High-end minimal. One idea per shot, lots of empty space, one accent color, one clean sans (Geist or Inter) with tight tracking. Masked type reveals, match cuts, one smooth camera language. Real footage only, never placeholder cards. No full stops in on-screen text.
Banned: shockwave rings, particle bursts, RGB split, camera shake, lens flares, neon glows, grid floors, flashing backgrounds, bouncy easing.
</direction>

<structure>
10 bars at 120 BPM, 2 seconds each.
Bar 1: the hook lands word by word on the beats.
Bar 2: one hook word morphs into the product UI. A cursor types and clicks.
The drop: a circle opens out of the button into a dark scene.
Then one move per bar: a wall of real clips with a scan line and 3 winners, the key output as big type, a 3D carousel of real videos with floor reflections and a motion-blurred whip onto one hero clip, the hero in a phone next to a panel that flips into results, big stats on push cuts, a 3-word ticker, a logo reveal, a fade to black.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file at 1920x1080. Every style is computed from time inside 
http://
window.seek(t): no CSS animations, no timers, no state between frames.
2. Real video: extract clips to 30fps JPEG sequences with ffmpeg and swap img sources per frame. seek awaits the image decodes.
3. Analyze the song with numpy: tempo, beat grid, energy per bar, the drop. Calibrate the grid to the real kick hits. Every cut sits on a downbeat, every UI hit on a beat.
4. Render with Playwright: 3 subframes per frame at t minus, at, and plus 1/240s, then blend with ffmpeg tmix for real motion blur at 60fps.
5. Place each sound effect so its measured peak, not its file start, lands on the event. Keep the effects quiet under the music. Loudnorm to -14 LUFS.
6. Probe 20 or more frames before the full render. Fix anything cluttered, overlapping or hard to read.
</build>

<gotchas>
Never set opacity or filter on a preserve-3d element, because it flattens and both faces show. Fade its wrapper instead. Measure element positions at runtime for match cuts. Only use music and sound effects whose license allows commercial use.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me a storyboard with every timing on the beat grid before you write any code.
</start>

author: techhalla
title: You are a world-class motion designer doing a 20.00s kinetic identity bump…
prompt:
You are a world-class motion designer doing a 20.00s kinetic identity bumper for TechHalla — an AI creator known for stealable workflows, not vibes. This piece must feel like the best designer in the room made a street-poster that moves. Showreel stakes: if this is weak, you don’t get hired.

DURATION: exactly 20.00 seconds. LOOPABLE: frame 0 == frame last (position, opacity, cursor if any).
FORMAT: one HTML file, 1080×1080 (square, X-native). 60fps.
PALETTE (strict):
- bg # 0A0A0A
- magenta # FF2BD6
- acid green # B8FF00
- white # F5F5F5 only for primary readable type when needed
No other hues. No gradients on UI chrome. Magenta/green may misregister (print offset) by 2–4px on impact frames only.

TYPE SYSTEM (use all three; never one font for everything):
1) Display / scream: Archivo Black (or equivalent ultra-condensed black) — 1–4 words max
2) Urban grotesque: Syne ExtraBold — secondary hits, stacked lines
3) Mono / “prompt code”: IBM Plex Mono Medium — small labels, timestamps, fake prompt crumbs
Tracking: display −40 to −80; mono +20. Optical kerning. No cute script fonts.

MESSAGE (locked — do not soften, do not add filler slogans):
Beat hits in this exact order:
1. STOP SCROLLING
2. AI VIDEO ISN’T EXPENSIVE
3. BAD PROMPTING IS
4. WORKFLOWS > WISHES
5. STEAL THE PROMPT
6. @ TECHHALLA
Supporting crumbs (mono, ≤18 chars, never full sentences): JSON · H3 · SEEDANCE · 0 KEYFRAMES · MAGNIFIC · COPY/PASTE

NARRATIVE ARC (20s):
0.0–2.5s  COLD OPEN — “STOP SCROLLING” slams in from below with spring overshoot; magenta smear trail; acid green baseline ticks across like a waveform.
2.5–6.5s  THESIS A — “AI VIDEO ISN’T EXPENSIVE” locks to a poster grid (baseline grid 8px). Letters scramble (seeded Fisher–Yates per glyph) then snap on the beat.
6.5–10.5s THESIS B — “BAD PROMPTING IS” replaces it via mask wipe through the letterforms (the outgoing line is the mask). Magenta/green channel split on the cut.
10.5–14.5s PROOF FLASH — rapid kinetic stack: WORKFLOWS > WISHES, then mono crumbs orbit a central block like a terminal. One fake “prompt block” types 3 lines max, then gets crossed by an acid green strikethrough that becomes a underline for STEAL THE PROMPT.
14.5–17.5s BRAND LOCK — @ TECHHALLA centers; display weight. A thick magenta bar and a thin acid green rule form an L-bracket mark (custom, not a logo download).
17.5–20.0s SETTLE / LOOP — hold lockup; micro-breath (scale 1.000→1.012→1.000); last frame == first ready for loop.

CONCRETE TECHNIQUES (required — implement, don’t approximate):
1. seek(t) pure function of time. No CSS transitions. No setInterval. No React state across frames.
2. Springs = closed-form step responses. Stack one spring per target change so motion stays deterministic.
3. Kinetic type: per-glyph spring (y, opacity, blur). Stagger = 1/16 note at 120 BPM (125ms).
4. Print misregistration: on accent frames only, duplicate text layer offset (±2–4px) in magenta and acid green at 40% opacity.
5. Mask reveal: destination text revealed by animating a path mask derived from the outgoing word’s outlines.
6. Camera: one orthographic camera; only punch-in (1.0→1.08) and horizontal smash-pans timed to beats — never random drift.
7. Motion blur: render 4 subframes per frame, blend (tmix-style).
8. Beat grid: 120 BPM, downbeat at t=0. Something must land on every beat for the first 16 beats; after that, every other beat is ok.
9. Pre-pass: before full render, export one still per major beat (8 frames). Fix cramped type, orphan words, low contrast — then render.

BANNED:
Generic AI clichés (brains, robots, neural nets, sparkles), soft gradients, bouncy cartoon easing, particle explosions, stock “futuristic HUD”, long paragraphs, narrator essay energy, Canva-deck energy, extra slogans beyond the locked message, purple/blue neon, glassmorphism.

If Astra already blew our minds… Opus 5.5 is a monster 😱

author: CurieuxExplorer
title: Type 1 Diabetes Interactive 3D Visualization
prompt:
Rebuild Type 1 diabetes in one HTML file, from the whole body down to a single molecule.

THE BROKEN MESSAGE

Type 1 diabetes isn't caused by sugar, weight or lifestyle. It's autoimmune: the immune system destroys the beta cells in the pancreas that make insulin.

Those cells live in tiny clusters called islets, about 1–2% of the pancreas. After a meal, they sense rising glucose and release insulin. Insulin signals muscle and fat to take glucose in, and tells the liver to release less.

In Type 1, that signal disappears.
The fuel is still there. The message is missing.
So glucose builds up in the blood.

With almost no insulin, the body breaks down fat fast and the liver makes ketones. They can build up into diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA), a medical emergency.

Insulin therapy doesn't cure Type 1. It replaces a signal the body can no longer provide adequately, through injections or a pump. The daily challenge is balance: too little and glucose rises, too much and it can fall dangerously low. Food, exercise, stress and timing all change the picture.

Technology helps. A CGM tracks glucose every few minutes, and automated insulin delivery (AID) adjusts insulin based on those readings.

In the build, you can compare Healthy vs Type 1 vs Type 1 + insulin on the same meal, drag one slider from INTACT to BROKEN to watch the signal fade, follow a glucose molecule through the body, and explore CGM, pumps and AID.

Type 1 diabetes changes the system.
It doesn't define the person.

Built in Three.js. Educational visualization, not medical advice.

title: Cinematic 3D rocket launch
prompt: Create a cinematic, highly detailed, interactive 3D rocket launch from an ocean platform at dawn. Deliver the complete project in one HTML file that opens directly in Chrome. Use Three.js + WebGL and procedural assets. Embed assets wherever practical; a reliable CDN may
postText:
prompt - 
Create a cinematic, highly detailed, interactive 3D rocket launch from an ocean platform at dawn. Deliver the complete project in one HTML file that opens directly in Chrome. Use Three.js + WebGL and procedural assets. Embed assets wherever practical; a reliable CDN may be used for the rendering library.

ART DIRECTION
Create a dramatic transition from a dark, blue-violet ocean before sunrise to warm sunlight above the atmosphere. Use convincing proportions, detailed materials, atmospheric depth, and carefully composed camera angles. The result should feel like a polished miniature spaceflight film.
ROCKET AND LAUNCH PLATFORM
Build a convincing multistage rocket with a shaped nose cone, panel seams, structural rings, interstage connections, engine nozzles, and a payload fairing that separates into two halves.

Create a detailed floating launch platform with a support tower, retracting strongback, service arms, railings, ladders, pipes, equipment, floodlights, and blinking warning beacons. Keep all structures physically connected and correctly positioned.
LAUNCH SEQUENCE
Create an approximately 46-second sequence:

Establishing camera move around the platform.

Service arms and strongback retract.
Engines ignite, illuminating the rocket, platform, and nearby water.
Smoke spreads across the deck as the rocket lifts off and accelerates.
The camera follows the climb from the atmosphere toward space.
The first stage separates and falls away.
The second-stage engine ignites.
The fairing halves separate, revealing a satellite.
The engine shuts down, the satellite deploys, and its solar panels unfold.
Finish with an orbital view of the satellite against Earth’s curved horizon and sunrise.
Compress the flight timeline for presentation while maintaining coherent motion. Avoid sudden position changes, intersecting components, or disconnected effects.
OCEAN, ATMOSPHERE, AND EFFECTS
Use animated shader-driven ocean waves with Fresnel reflections and warm engine-light reflections. Create layered exhaust with a bright core, softer outer flame, and drifting smoke particles.
Smoke should expand, fade, and respond to wind. Exhaust must remain attached to the correct engine through staging. Transition smoothly from atmospheric haze to a dark star field and Earth’s illuminated limb.

CAMERA AND INTERACTION
Use smooth cinematic camera transitions: wide establishing view, low-angle ignition shot, ascent tracking, stage separation, and satellite close-up. Keep the main subject visible in both portrait and landscape layouts.

Include play/pause, replay, and a scrubber with event markers. Seeking must reconstruct the correct rocket configuration, particle state, camera position, and lighting. Replaying must reset the entire sequence cleanly.
Keep the interface minimal and unobtrusive. Allow it to be hidden for recording.

TECHNICAL QUALITY
Use frame-rate-independent animation and efficient particle systems. Reuse geometry and materials where appropriate, handle resizing correctly, and balance visual detail with smooth performance.

Test the final HTML in a desktop browser. Inspect the console and capture screenshots at ignition, liftoff, staging, and satellite deployment. Fix loading errors, clipping, geometry problems, broken seeking, and poor camera framing before delivering the file.

author: twoclipping
title: Ask me for: 8 to 12 UI states I want the shape to become (e.g. button, loa…
prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for: 8 to 12 UI states I want the shape to become (e.g. button, loader, player, slider, toggle, tabs, chart, command palette, toast), pure black and white or one accent color, and a royalty-free song around 120 BPM (e.g. Mixkit, free for commercial use).
</inputs>

<direction>
Dribbble-level UI motion. One shape, never cut: every state is the same element morphing its size, radius and color while its content swaps with a short blur. A cursor drives every change with real clicks and drags. Light warm-gray canvas, black and white components, one clean UI font (Geist). Springs everywhere, a tiny overshoot at most. The camera zooms so each state fills the frame. The last frame is the first frame, so it loops.
Banned: bouncy easing, particle bursts, glows, gradients on UI chrome, mismatched icon strokes, dead time, anything that looks like a template.
</direction>

<structure>
120 BPM, 7 bars, something happens on every beat.
Button → loader → check → dynamic island → music player with a play/pause morph → scrub the progress bar → it becomes a volume slider that stretches when dragged past max → a toggle flips on the beat → the knob becomes a liquid tab indicator → the tabs open into a chart that draws itself, with a tooltip on hover → it collapses into ⌘K → type to filter → enter → toast → back to the button.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file, square 1440x1440. Every style is computed from time inside seek(t): no CSS transitions, no timers, no state carried between frames.
2. Springs are closed-form step responses. A value that changes target many times is the sum of one spring per change, so it stays a pure function of time.
3. The tab indicator's two edges ride different springs, so the leading edge stretches ahead of the trailing one. Same trick for the toggle knob.
4. Drags are direct manipulation: while the cursor is held, the value is computed from its position. On release it springs back from wherever it was.
5. Analyze the song with numpy for the beat grid and start on a downbeat. Place every UI sound by its measured peak.
6. Render with Playwright: 4 subframes per frame, blended with ffmpeg tmix for motion blur at 60fps.
7. Render one frame per beat before the full render. Fix anything off the grid, cramped or hard to read.
</build>

<gotchas>
Never put will-change on anything the camera scales or the text renders blurry. Text that swaps inside a morphing container needs its own enter and exit timing or it overlaps. Make the last frame identical to the first, cursor position and speed included, or the loop stutters.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me the state list on the beat grid before you write any code.
</start>

Using HyperFrames, make a hype teaser for the product in this post - [link]. Landscape, around 27 seconds. Match the product UI, wallpaper and copy from the post's video

postText:
prompt for this: 

# PROJECT: "UNFINISHED" (未完) — The Unfinished Ronin
A 90-second, fast-paced, cinematic sumi-e ink film rendered in code, third-person camera

## MISSION
Build a 90-second film in which every frame looks like a living Japanese ink painting,
painted as we watch, following one character, the Ronin, through a violent cold open,
a desperate chase, a duel with his perfect opposite, and a profound ending.

The film must succeed on four levels at once:
1. ACTION: fights as thrilling, readable and brutal as the best animated sword duels ever
   made. Fast, rhythmic, no wasted seconds.
2. ANIMATION: character motion at the level of a top feature animation studio. Weight,
   arcs, timing, anticipation, follow-through. Not one foot slides, not one frame jitters.
3. ART: every paused frame must look like a genuine sumi-e painting on real washi, with
   vermilion accents, not a shader or filter.
4. MEANING: a viewer with no words or explanation must understand the story and feel its
   theme by the final frame.

Judge every decision against one question: "Would a master sumi-e painter, a lead
animator at a top studio, and a great action director all pause the frame and nod?"

This is incredibly ambitious on purpose. You will work autonomously across many
iterations and sessions. You will not stop when it "looks decent." You stop only when
the exit criteria at the bottom are met and proven with captured frames.

## THEME (every shot must serve this)
To be unfinished is to be alive. Completion is stillness; stillness is death. No one
finishes you. You pick up the brush yourself.
- Mujō (impermanence): the painted world fades behind the Ronin. Nothing lasts, and that
  is what makes it beautiful.
- Ma (meaningful emptiness): blank paper is possibility, not nothing. The final image is
  mostly empty paper, and it must feel hopeful.
- Perfection vs. life: the Finished One's flawless strokes are beautiful but dead. The
  Ronin's rough, splattering strokes are imperfect but alive.

## HARD RULES
1. 100% original characters, story and designs. Nothing recognizable from existing films,
   games or anime.
2. All geometry, textures and animation are authored or generated in code. No downloaded
   models, textures or motion capture.
3. No dialogue, no voice. At most three pieces of on-screen calligraphy.
4. Palette: ink blacks and greys on washi, plus VERMILION (shu-iro, about #C8322B) used
   only as specified in the RED INK section. Every red mark must mean something.
5. No gore. Enemies are made of ink. Wounds on the Ronin reveal blank paper.
6. Never claim something looks or moves well without captured frames proving it.
7. Never delete or simplify a working system to "fix" a bug. Fix the cause.
8. Fully deterministic: fixed timestep, seeded randomness, so every frame renders
   identically every time. Review depends on this.
9. Maintain PROGRESS.md, STORY.md and ANIMATION.md at all times. A fresh session must be
   able to resume cold from them.

## THE CHARACTERS

### The Ronin (protagonist)
Lean, tired, deadly. Moves like a real swordsman: economical, grounded, explosive.
- Wide straw kasa hat, cracked along one edge, with frayed ties that react to every
  movement and gust.
- Tattered haori over kimono, loose hakama that flare and snap in motion, straw sandals,
  one katana with a worn wrapped hilt.
- A single faded RED THREAD tied around the hat cord: the only color the painter gave him.
  A hint that he was loved, never explained.
- His FACE IS BLANK PAPER. Under the hat, only the faint suggestion of a jaw line.
- His LEFT ARM IS UNFINISHED: faint grey underdrawing, loose sketch lines, construction
  circles. It works like a real arm but is visibly incomplete.
- His sword is always the darkest mark in the frame: scorched ink, glossy near-black.
- Brushwork: wild, fast, expressive. His strokes splatter, break into dry brush and bleed.

### The Finished One — Kanzen (完全, "perfect / complete")
The painter's masterpiece. Not a villain: a tragic figure who believes completion is
peace.
- Ornate samurai armor, every lacing and plate painted with flawless precision.
- A fully painted, serene face. His eyes never blink.
- A vermilion seal stamped on his chest plate. He carries a vermilion seal stone.
- Brushwork: perfect, even, controlled strokes with crisp edges. No splatter, no dry brush.
- Motion: absolute stillness, then instant perfect movement, then stillness again. Like a
  statue that only moves to strike. Rain does not touch him.

### The Blots
The painter's rejected drafts: splattered mistakes, crossed-out half-warriors with
strike-through lines across their bodies, smudged limbs. They crawl out of blank paper.
Their motion is deliberately wrong: jerky, scribbled, on uneven frame timing. When cut
they burst into splatter that bleeds into the paper.

### The Brush (the unseen painter)
A giant brush tip descending from above the frame, painting the world just ahead of the
Ronin. We never see the hand or the painter. Its strokes are confident early, then grow
thin and shaky as the film goes on: the painter is failing.

## RED INK — the color has its own story arc
Vermilion begins as the color of stillness and ends as the color of life. Keep it rare:
no more than about 8% of any frame, except the climax burst.
1. COLD OPEN: a pale red sun disc behind the bridge, softly bleeding into wet paper.
   Beautiful, and quietly ominous.
2. THROUGHOUT: the faded red thread on the Ronin's hat cord, catching the eye in motion.
3. THE VILLAGE: every frozen villager bears a small vermilion seal. Red = finished = still.
4. KANZEN: his chest seal and seal stone, the most saturated red so far.
5. THE DUEL: the seal stone grazes the Ronin's sleeve, leaving a vermilion smear on him.
   Completion is trying to claim him.
6. THE FINAL STROKE: as the Ronin swings the fallen brush, it drags through the smear on
   his sleeve and loads with vermilion. The final stroke is black ink with a living red
   core: the only stroke in the film that is both.
7. THE RELEASE: when the seals crack, they burst into vermilion ink that falls across the
   village as red PLUM BLOSSOMS (a classic sumi-e subject, painted with single red dots
   and fine black stamens). Red transforms from seals into blossoms: from stillness to life.
8. THE ENDING: one red blossom drifts onto the Ronin's hat, beside the red thread. The seal
   corner of the scroll stays empty.

Red ink behaves differently from black: cinnabar is more opaque, slightly granular, sits
on top of black ink rather than mixing, and bleeds less. Simulate that difference.

## STORY AND SHOT LIST — 90 seconds, fast-paced
Pacing target: average shot length about 2 seconds during action, with deliberate longer
holds (3–5s) for the three emotional beats. The contrast is what makes both work.
Build a rhythm map: tension rises in waves, each wave ending in a bigger hit.

### COLD OPEN — "The Stroke" (0–15s) — must hook in the first 1.5 seconds
0.0–1.5s: Pure white washi. The sound of a brush dipping into ink. Then a single violent
  horizontal black stroke rips across the frame with a sharp swish. It is a sword cut.
1.5–3.5s: Whip-pull back into third-person over the Ronin's shoulder. He's mid-battle in
  heavy rain on a narrow wooden bridge over a void of blank paper. A pale red sun bleeds
  behind him. Twelve Blots swarm from both ends.
3.5–11.0s: One continuous third-person combat take (hidden cuts allowed on whip pans):
  - He ducks a lunging Blot, cuts it in half on the way up. Splatter.
  - Spins, two-cut combination through two more. Hakama snaps with the spin.
  - A Blot grabs his sketched left arm; he kicks it off the bridge into blank paper.
  - Slides under a leaping pair, cuts both mid-air. Slow-motion splatter for 12 frames,
    then back to full speed.
  - The bridge behind him is fading into blank paper, and the Blots keep crawling out of
    that blankness. He is fighting AND running out of world.
11.0–13.0s: The last Blot leaps at him. He draws low and cuts upward in a single iai
  stroke. Hit-stop, then one inverted "negative" impact frame (white ink on black), then
  back. The splatter hangs in the air.
13.0–15.0s: The hanging splatter drifts, bleeds and resolves into 未完, with "UNFINISHED"
  in small grey type beneath. He flicks the ink off his blade (chiburi) and sheathes it
  slowly (nōtō). Click. One beat of silence.

### ACT I — "The Chase" (15–35s)
15–22s: The bridge fades out from under him and he runs. Third-person trailing shot, low
  and fast. Ahead, the Brush paints a bamboo forest in rapid strokes just before he
  reaches it; behind him, the world fades, and the Blots pour out of the blankness in
  pursuit. He is racing the brush.
22–25s: Two Blots burst out of the mist ahead. Two cuts, 1.5 seconds, without breaking
  stride. The camera whips around him in a half orbit and back to trailing.
25–29s: EMOTIONAL BEAT 1 (hold). He skids to a stop at a still pool. The pursuit sound
  drops away. His reflection shows only the hat and blank paper where a face should be.
  He lifts his sketched left hand and looks at it. Rain drops ripple the reflection.
29–35s: A village in mist. Its people are fully painted and frozen mid-motion: a child
  mid-laugh, a woman pouring tea with the stream suspended in the air, a merchant mid-bow.
  Each bears a vermilion seal. He walks between them. Only rain. The camera weaves slowly
  through the frozen figures. Hard cut to:

### ACT II — "The Finished One" (35–65s)
35–39s: EMOTIONAL BEAT 2 (hold). A courtyard. Kanzen stands perfectly still, rain
  not touching him. Kanzen raises the seal stone and holds it out: an offer. "Let me
  finish you, and you will never fade." The Ronin looks at his sketched hand. Then he
  slowly draws his sword. Refusal.

THE DUEL (39–65s). Two brushwork styles colliding. Real kenjutsu throughout: distance,
timing, feints, blade binds, sliding footwork. Choreograph every move in ANIMATION.md.
39–43s: EXCHANGE 1. Kanzen strikes first: an instant perfect stroke appears in the air.
  The Ronin barely parries. Black ink flecks fly from the blade contact like sparks. He is
  driven back, sandals skidding across wet stone.
43–49s: EXCHANGE 2. The Ronin attacks: a five-cut flurry, wild, splattering, dry-brush
  trails across the frame. Kanzen deflects each one with minimal movement and returns to
  stillness between blocks. The fifth deflection spins the Ronin around.
49–53s: EXCHANGE 3. Kanzen's counter: one horizontal cut across the Ronin's chest.
  Hit-stop, negative frame. The wound reveals blank paper, and its edges begin to creep
  outward. He is being erased.
53–58s: EXCHANGE 4. Kanzen lunges with the seal stone at his heart. The Ronin deflects it
  with his sketched arm; the stone grazes his sleeve and leaves a vermilion smear. The
  force throws him across the courtyard into a pool of ink. He rises to one knee.
58–65s: Above, the Brush falters. Its strokes go thin and shaky, then stop. The world
  begins to fade everywhere at once: the walls, the village, even Kanzen's edges. Kanzen
  raises the seal for the final strike. Above them, the Brush slips.

### ACT III — "The Brush" (65–80s)
65–68s: The Brush falls in slow motion, spinning, flinging droplets. It lands and rolls
  to the Ronin's sketched left hand.
68–71s: EMOTIONAL BEAT 3 (hold). He grips it. As his fingers close, the underdrawing of
  his hand darkens into real ink for the first time, from fingertips up to the shoulder.
71–75s: Kanzen strikes with the seal. The Ronin rises and swings the brush; it drags
  through the vermilion smear on his sleeve and loads with red. He paints one enormous
  stroke across the whole frame: an ensō-like arc of black ink with a living red core. It
  meets the seal. The seal cracks.
75–80s: Kanzen does not die. His perfect strokes soften and bleed. For the first time,
  his painted eyes blink. His face shows relief. He dissolves into a soft grey wash, free.
  Across the village, every seal cracks and bursts into vermilion ink that falls as red
  plum blossoms. The tea finally pours. The child finishes laughing.

### EPILOGUE — "Ma" (80–90s)
80–85s: Third-person trailing shot, the reverse of Act I: the Ronin walks into blank
  paper, and HE paints the world ahead with the brush, trailing ink. His face is still
  blank. A single red blossom drifts down and settles on his hat beside the red thread.
85–88s: The camera rises and pulls back, higher and higher, revealing the whole film as
  one long painted scroll, the Ronin a tiny figure at its unfinished edge.
88–90s: The seal corner of the scroll stays empty. A faint grey 未完 appears there. Fade
  to white paper. Rain, then silence.

## THIRD-PERSON CAMERA LANGUAGE
Shot like the most cinematic third-person action games, reinterpreted as painting:
- DEFAULT: follow cam 3–4 m behind, slightly above, over the right shoulder, 35mm.
  Spring-damped lag so it feels operated, never locked. Subtle procedural handheld drift.
- COMBAT: widens to 24–28mm, orbits to keep the Ronin and the current threat both framed,
  and drifts toward incoming attacks a beat early so the viewer reads them.
- WHIP PANS: used to cut between attackers, painted as streaks of dry-brush motion blur.
- IMPACT: 2–4 frame hit-stop, camera kick along the strike direction, and on the four
  biggest hits only, a single inverted negative frame.
- SLOW MOTION: ramped smoothly, never abrupt, used only for splatter, the falling brush,
  and the final stroke.
- EMOTIONAL BEATS: the camera stops following and holds. Lens lengthens to 85–135mm.
  Stillness in the camera means something is important.
- Composition follows sumi-e: asymmetry, generous empty space, the Ronin often small in a
  large field of paper. Action must read even as a tiny thumbnail.

## ANIMATION STANDARD
Every frame of character motion must meet feature-animation quality:
- The 12 principles, applied with discipline: anticipation before every strike, follow-
  through and overlap after, slow-in and slow-out, clean arcs, strong staging, weight.
- Real swordwork: correct stances (chūdan, hassō, waki-gamae), sliding footwork
  (suri-ashi), cuts driven from the hips, the draw cut, chiburi and nōtō.
- Weight: every step transfers weight through the hips; landings compress the knees;
  heavy hits push the body back.
- Secondary motion: hakama, haori sleeves, hat ties and the red thread lag and settle
  with convincing cloth dynamics.
- Breathing whenever the Ronin is still: a subtle rise and fall of the shoulders.
- Contrast of motion styles is storytelling: the Ronin is fluid and alive; Kanzen is
  stillness broken by instant perfect motion; the Blots move on uneven, scribbled timing.
- Key poses must read as pure black silhouettes. If a pose doesn't read as a silhouette,
  it doesn't work.

## INK REALISM — real ink on real paper
The target is not photorealism. It is ink that a master would believe was painted by
hand. Every effect below is simulated, not faked with a filter.

### Paper
- Procedural washi: long visible kozo fibers, subtle thickness variation, a warm
  off-white tone, faint tooth visible under thin washes.
- The paper is the canvas, fixed to the screen like a real sheet. Intentional.
- Ink diffuses along fiber direction (anisotropic).

### Ink behavior
- Five tones of black: scorched (glossy near-black), dark, heavy, light, clear. Tone
  expresses depth: foreground dark and sharp, background pale and soft.
- Nijimi: wet ink bleeding into paper with feathered edges that keep spreading briefly
  after a stroke lands (GPU diffusion on a wetness field).
- Edge darkening as washes dry: pigment migrates to the rim.
- Kasure (dry brush): bristles separate when ink runs low or the stroke is fast.
- Bokashi: smooth graded washes for mist, sky and distance.
- Granulation: fine pigment speckle in pale washes.
- Pooling where strokes start or pause, tapered lift where they end.
- Splatter with main drops and satellite droplets, each bleeding where it lands.
- Drying: fresh ink has a faint wet sheen that dulls over a few seconds.
- Vermilion behaves as described in the RED INK section.

### Brush strokes
- Every line is a real brush stroke: pressure along its length, bristle texture, ink
  load that decreases along the stroke (long strokes end in dry brush), speed affecting
  width and dryness.
- Stroke anatomy: pressed entry, confident body, tapered exit.
- Linework is derived from 3D geometry (silhouettes, creases, contours) chained into
  brush strokes anchored to the objects so they never swim. Controlled "boil" on
  linework at 12 fps for a hand-painted feel; everything else at full frame rate.
- Interior form uses washes, not outlines: lighting is converted to ink tones.

### Painting-in and fading
- The Brush paints the world in a real painter's order: main structural strokes first,
  then secondary strokes, then detail touches and dots.
- Fading is not a crossfade: ink lightens, loses its edges, sinks into the paper fibers
  until only a faint ghost remains, then nothing.

### Weather and atmosphere
- Rain as fine, fast, pale dry strokes, denser in front, with some drops bleeding where
  they hit painted surfaces.
- Mist as layered pale washes with parallax.
- Wind moves bamboo, hat ties, sleeves, hakama and the red thread.

## SOUND
Procedural Web Audio, fast and punchy in action, with silence used as an instrument.
- Brush: dipping, dragging on paper, bristles lifting. Every painted stroke has a sound.
- Sword: cut swishes, sharp metallic rings on contact, the sheath click. Every blade
  contact must land on the exact frame of contact.
- Blots: wet, smeary, scratchy sounds.
- Rain, wind through bamboo, distant thunder.
- Music: taiko-like drums driving the cold open, chase and duel; a breathy flute tone for
  the three emotional beats; one low sustained tone when the brush falls; drums drop out
  completely at the final stroke, leaving only the sound of the brush.
- First sound of the film: a brush dipping into ink. Last sound: rain fading to silence.

## TECH STACK
- Three.js (latest), WebGPU renderer with WebGL2 fallback. Vite dev server.
- Custom sumi-e NPR pipeline:
  1. G-buffer: depth, normals, object IDs, lighting, surface-direction field.
  2. Line pass: silhouettes, creases and contours chained into polylines and rendered with
     the stroke model.
  3. Wash pass: lighting converted into the five ink tones, painted as wet washes.
  4. Ink simulation: GPU wetness and pigment diffusion on the paper (nijimi, edge
     darkening, granulation, drying), with separate behavior for vermilion.
  5. Paint-in and fade system driven by the Brush and time.
  6. Composite on procedural washi.
- Characters built procedurally in code on skinned skeletons, animated with hand-authored
  keyframes, procedural IK for foot planting, and cloth simulation.
- Two render modes:
  - REAL-TIME: 30+ fps at 1080p for interactive playback and scrubbing.
  - FILM MODE: renders frame by frame at maximum quality (more simulation steps,
    supersampling, full-resolution diffusion) at 1080p or 4K, 24 fps, then encodes to MP4
    with ffmpeg. This is the final deliverable.
- Headless, deterministic capture via Playwright.
- lil-gui debug panel with toggles for every pass, and a timeline scrubber.

## FILE STRUCTURE
/src/characters/  ronin, kanzen, blots, brush
/src/anim/        skeleton, IK, cloth, choreography, timeline
/src/world/       bridge, bamboo, pool, village, courtyard, scroll
/src/ink/         stroke model, line extraction, washes, diffusion, vermilion, paint-in, fade
/src/paper/       washi generation
/src/camera/      follow cam, combat cam, whip pans, hit-stop, impact frames, shot list
/src/audio/
/tools/capture.ts      frames, sequences, contact sheets, onion skins, silhouettes
/tools/anim-checks.ts  automated animation quality checks
/tools/checks.ts       performance, console errors, determinism, timeline integrity
/tools/render-film.ts  film mode export to MP4
/review/               captured material per iteration
PROGRESS.md
STORY.md       every beat: what the viewer sees, hears and should feel
ANIMATION.md   move-by-move choreography, key poses, timing charts per shot

## PRODUCTION PIPELINE (in order; do not skip ahead)
(A) INK LAB: stroke model, washes, diffusion, vermilion, paper. Paint test sheets (a
    bamboo stalk, a stone, a splatter, a plum branch with red blossoms) until single
    frames look genuinely hand-painted. Everything depends on this.
(B) ANIMATIC: the entire 90 seconds with grey block characters, final cameras, final
    timing and temp sound. Lock pacing here. It must already be exciting as grey boxes.
(C) BLOCKING: key poses for every shot, stepped (no interpolation), checked as
    silhouettes.
(D) SPLINE: interpolated motion, arcs cleaned, timing refined.
(E) POLISH: overlap, cloth, breathing, micro-motion, contact frames, hit-stops.
(F) INK RENDER: full sumi-e pipeline applied to the finished animation, shot by shot,
    starting with the cold open.
(G) RED, SOUND AND FINISHING: vermilion arc, full sound design, final pacing.
(H) FILM MODE EXPORT: final MP4.

## THE PERFECTION LOOP
Every iteration, without exception:

1. BUILD: implement the next highest-priority item from PROGRESS.md.

2. CAPTURE (deterministic): for every shot you touched, render
   - a frame-by-frame sequence of the shot,
   - a contact sheet (every 3rd frame),
   - onion skins: 8 consecutive frames overlaid, to judge spacing and arcs,
   - arc traces: the paths of the sword tip, both wrists, hips and head drawn over the
     shot, to check they are clean curves,
   - silhouette renders of every key pose (solid black on white),
   - one full-resolution "gallery still."
   Also, every iteration, render one middle frame of every shot in the film, in order,
   as a storyboard strip. Save everything to /review/iter_NNN/.

3. AUTOMATED CHECKS (tools/anim-checks.ts): report and fail the iteration on
   - foot sliding: a planted foot moving more than 2 mm per frame,
   - joint limits exceeded,
   - interpenetration: blade through body, limbs through limbs, cloth through body,
   - jitter: acceleration spikes in any joint or camera between consecutive frames,
   - popping: sudden pose changes not motivated by a cut or hit-stop,
   - sync: every blade contact aligned with its sound and hit-stop to the exact frame,
   - pacing: shot lengths vs. the targets in STORY.md.

4. CRITIQUE: actually look at every captured image. Score 1–10:
   a. Animation (weighted double): weight, arcs, timing, anticipation, follow-through,
      silhouette clarity, real swordwork.
   b. Ink authenticity (weighted double): would a sumi-e master believe a human painted
      it? Bleeding, dry brush, tone, stroke anatomy, paper.
   c. Action and pacing: clarity, impact, rhythm, no wasted seconds, holds that land.
   d. Third-person camera: operated, cinematic, purposeful, action always readable.
   e. Composition: asymmetry, empty space, focal clarity, thumbnail readability.
   f. Red ink: every red mark meaningful, the arc from stillness to life clear.
   g. Story clarity: could someone with no explanation describe what just happened?
   h. Emotional impact: does the moment make you feel what STORY.md says it should?
   i. Gut check: "Painting or shader?" and "Animated by a master or by a program?"
      Write one sentence each on the single biggest tell.

5. LOG: append to PROGRESS.md the iteration number, all scores, check results, the two
   biggest tells, the weakest moment in the film so far (timestamp and why), what
   changed, performance, and a ranked list of the next 3 fixes.

6. FIX: failed automated checks first. Then the lowest-scoring category, at its root
   cause. Then go back to step 1.

Self-critique rules:
- Common tells of fake ink: uniform line width, untapered lines, edges too clean, flat
  washes, no paper showing through thin ink, splatter without satellites, strokes
  swimming, everything the same darkness, red that looks like a digital overlay.
- Common tells of weak animation: floaty motion with no weight, even spacing (no easing),
  broken arcs, poses that don't read as silhouettes, everything moving at once with no
  overlap, sword hits without impact, idle characters frozen instead of breathing.
- Every 5 iterations, do a FRESH EYES pass: view the storyboard strip in order as if
  seeing it for the first time, and write what the story seems to be about and where
  attention drifts. If it doesn't match the THEME, fix the story before the visuals.
- Every 5 iterations, do a PACING pass: list every shot with its length and energy level
  (1–10), and check the rhythm map rises in waves with contrast between action and holds.
- If a score stalls for 3 iterations, change the approach, not the parameters.
- Every moment must earn its place. Cut or rework anything that doesn't serve the action,
  the art or the meaning.

title: Yohaku Short Film
prompt:
three.jsで、縦長1080×1920・30コマ/秒・約36秒の短編映像を作ってください。

【作品名】
余白

【見せたい体験】
効率化に追われて時間を失っていく感覚と、余白を手に入れた瞬間に人生が豊かな光で満たされていく感覚を、人物を一切登場させずに体感させる映像です。最後に床一面に浮かび上がるステンドグラスの光で、見た人が思わず息をのむことを目指します。

【舞台】
・薄暗い石造りの大聖堂の内部。正面の壁に、高さ15m・幅10mの尖頭アーチ型の窓が一つだけある
・窓の外からは、斜め45度の角度で強い光が差し込み、石の床に窓の形の光を落としている
・窓には、中央に聖母、両脇に翼を広げた二人の天使、上部にバラ窓を配したステンドグラスがはまっている。デザインは既存の作品を模さずオリジナルで、左右対称の構図にする

【時間の構成】
0〜3秒：窓から差す光は、まだ色のない白い光。床にやわらかな白い光の形
3〜11秒：「忙しい」「効率化」「至急」「締切」などの言葉が刻まれた灰色の立方体が、部屋の手前から次々と飛んできて窓を埋めていく。飛来のペースはどんどん加速し、窓が埋まるほど部屋は暗くなる
11〜14秒：窓は完全にふさがれ、闇と静寂
14〜19秒：「忙しい」のブロックが一つだけ窓から外れて落ち、光の粒になって消える。空いた穴から、鮮やかな色の一筋の光が差し込む
19〜26秒：最初の穴を中心に、ブロックが連鎖的に外れていく。穴が増えるたびに色とりどりの光の柱が増え、隠れていたステンドグラスが少しずつ姿を現す
26〜33秒：すべてのブロックが消え、カメラは光の柱をくぐり抜けて上昇し、真上から床を見下ろす。床一面に、聖母と天使のステンドグラスが色鮮やかな光として映し出されている
33〜36秒：画面全体がまばゆい光に包まれ、最後の言葉が浮かび、静かに終わる

【言葉（明朝体、控えめに浮かんでは消える）】
・「毎日、もっと速く。」
・「もっと、効率よく。」
・「気づけば、光が入らなくなっていた。」
・「ひとつ、手放してみる。」
・「空いたところから、光が入る。」
・「その光は、前より豊かだった。」
・最後に大きく：「豊かさは余白に宿る」

【光と質感】
・光の柱は、ステンドグラスのその場所の色に染まり、空中の塵がきらめく
・床の投影は、窓のどの穴が空いているかを正確に反映する（ブロックがある場所は影になる）
・ブロックは無機質なマットグレー。言葉は白く刻印されている
・前半は冷たく無彩色、後半は宝石のような赤・青・金。この色の対比で「豊かになった」ことを語る

【技術条件】
・ステンドグラスの絵柄は画像として生成し、床の光・光の柱・窓の表示はすべて同じ絵柄から計算して一致させる
・時間を1/30秒ずつ正確に進めて1コマずつ書き出し、MP4にする

【仕上げ】
各場面を実際に描画して確認し、ステンドグラスの絵柄が床の上で聖母と天使として読み取れるか、言葉が読めるか、動きが唐突でないかを直してから渡してください。

title: Build a racing game inspired by Ignition (1997): angled top-down camera, a…
prompt:
Build a racing game inspired by Ignition (1997): angled top-down camera, arcade-leaning
physics, vehicles with very distinct personalities. This must be an original game,
not a copy. Use an original name, an original track, and zero original assets.

## Stack
- Vite + TypeScript (strict), Three.js for rendering, no UI framework
  (HUD in plain DOM/CSS).
- Low-poly graphics generated in code (BoxGeometry, CylinderGeometry, etc.),
  no external models or textures. Solid colors and simple materials.
- Custom simplified 2.5D physics (movement on the XZ plane, height from terrain).
  No physics engine.

## Architecture
- src/game/ (game loop with fixed timestep), src/vehicles/, src/track/, src/ai/,
  src/render/, src/ui/
- Vehicles are data-driven: mass, power, top speed, grip, steering, collision
  resistance, and boost parameters (strength, duration, recharge time).
  One Vehicle class, different configurations.
- Any vehicle can be controlled by either the player or the AI
  (shared control interface: throttle, brake, steer, boost).
- Track as data: centerline spline + width + list of zones
  (ice, shortcut, obstacle). Generate the road mesh and AI waypoints from it.

## Vehicles (original names, no brands)
Four vehicles. The player picks one on the selection screen; the remaining 3
are driven by the AI.
- 90s-style police sedan (black and white, light bar): heavy, stable,
  pushes hard in collisions.
- Muscle car convertible: fastest on straights, oversteers in corners.
- Red monster truck: slow, but ignores bumps and rams everything else.
- Postal delivery van: slow, high center of gravity, sways in corners.
The handling differences must be clearly noticeable. All four must be playable
and competitive. Slower vehicles compensate with e.g. collision resistance,
terrain handling, or a stronger or more frequent boost.

## Boost
- Every vehicle has a boost: a short, pronounced acceleration beyond its
  normal top speed.
- Boost charges automatically from 0 to 100%. It can only be used at 100%.
  After use, the meter drops to 0 and starts charging again.
- Strength, duration and recharge time are unique to each vehicle
  (e.g. muscle car: short and very strong; van: weaker but recharges fast;
  monster truck: long but slow to recharge).
- Visual effect while boosting: exhaust flame or trail, slight camera
  pull-back.
- The AI also uses boost, sensibly: on straights, not before sharp corners
  or on ice.

## Track
A mountain town with a Canadian feel, winter turning into spring thaw:
- closed loop, roughly 60–90 seconds per lap
- a waterfall visible from the track and a wooden bridge over a river
- a railroad crossing with a train passing periodically
  (collision = strong knockback, not game over)
- ice patches with reduced grip
- one shortcut (tight, risky); decorations: spruce trees, wooden houses, snow
- barriers or natural obstacles so vehicles can't get stuck off the track.
  Failsafe: if a vehicle (including bots) is stuck for more than ~4 s,
  automatically return it to the track at the last checkpoint.

## Gameplay
- 3 laps, standing grid start, 3-2-1 countdown
- AI follows waypoints with a driving style that depends on the vehicle,
  light rubber-banding, avoids obstacles, no teleporting (except the
  failsafe track return described above)
- Sliding comes purely from physics (grip, speed, ice), no handbrake
- Camera: top-down at ~50°, follows the player with a slight look-ahead
  in the direction of travel
- Controls: arrows/WASD (throttle, brake/reverse, steering), space = boost
- Screens: start → vehicle selection (model preview + stat bars, including
  boost) → race → results → restart (with option to change vehicle)

## HUD
- Position, lap, lap time, best lap, minimap.
- Boost meter styled as a car battery: rectangular casing with two terminals
  (+/−) on top, fill level rises as it charges. Color shifts from red through
  yellow to green. At 100% the battery clearly signals readiness (pulsing or
  glow, "BOOST" label or lightning bolt icon). While boosting, the meter
  drains quickly.

## Out of scope for v1
Sound, options menu, multiple tracks, multiplayer, save state.

## Workflow
1. First propose a plan and file structure, then implement in stages:
   (a) game loop + one vehicle on a flat plane, including boost,
   (b) track, (c) remaining vehicles and AI, (d) obstacles and train,
   (e) vehicle selection, HUD with battery meter, and screens.
2. After each stage run `npm run build` and fix type errors.
3. Add unit tests (Vitest) for vehicle physics, boost logic (charging,
   lockout below 100%, reset after use), and lap/position logic.
4. Finally: a README describing the controls and how to add a new track
   or vehicle.

## Acceptance criteria
`npm install && npm run dev` launches the game. You can pick any of the 4
vehicles and complete 3 laps against 3 bots. Each vehicle handles differently
and has a noticeably different boost. Boost only works with a full battery,
and bots use it too. The train and ice work. Results show the correct order.
Stable 60 FPS on an average laptop.

author: itsolelehmann
title: 4 seasons passing outside a train window, a cozy carriage, a cup of coffee…
prompt: 4 seasons passing outside a train window, a cozy carriage, a cup of coffee on the table, Grand Budapest Hotel style
postText:
Anthropic has no image or video model, yet Opus 5.5 just made me this 30 second animated film using nothing but 2,800 lines of code

(yes, this is 100% Claude Code with no other AI tools, connectors, or reference images)

i gave it one prompt: 4 seasons passing outside a train window, a cozy carriage, a cup of coffee on the table, Grand Budapest Hotel style

and it literally came back with the finished .mp4 file ready in the chat

so i asked it... how did you achieve this result when you have no image model??

here's what Claude actually does behind the scenes:

1. sets up free drawing software on your computer, the kind that turns written instructions into pixels

2. writes ~2,800 lines of code describing every object as shapes with exact coordinates: a tree is a brown trunk plus ~6 overlapping green circles, the coffee cup is a few ovals and curves

3. layers the scenery at different speeds, so telegraph poles whip past 140x faster than the mountains (which is what gives it depth)

4. renders a still of each season, looks at them, then fixes what looks off

5. animates it like a flipbook: it calculates where every object should be at each moment, then redraws the whole scene 900 times

6. builds the soundtrack the same way, as equations. a plucked string is a stack of sound waves that fade out. each rail click lands on the exact frame where the coffee ripples

7. stitches it all into the final video

it even invented its own season transitions: a passing train sweeps spring into summer, tunnel turns autumn into winter, etc

the creativity and attention to detail is getting pretty ridiculous

author: GodsBoy7777
title: Marble Computer Animation
prompt:
Build a single self-contained HTML file: a 3D marble computer, in the spirit of Wintergatan's marble machine and the Digi-Comp II, that adds two 4-bit numbers using nothing but marbles falling through mechanical toggles.

Hard rules:

1. One HTML file. Three.js from https://t.co/KCQbEZLusb via an import map, plus its OrbitControls addon. No other libraries, no physics engine, no external assets.

2. The mechanism is the computer. Each bit of the result is stored in a two-state toggle (flip-flop) that a marble physically flips as it passes. Carries happen because a marble leaving one toggle rolls on to the next. Do not compute the answer in JavaScript arithmetic anywhere. The displayed result must be read from the toggle states after the last marble stops.

3. Marbles move along tracks with believable gravity and timing. Nothing teleports. You may script motion along paths, but every toggle flip must be caused by a marble arriving at it.

4. Input: two rows of four switches (A and B, 0 to 15), set by clicking. A lever labelled RUN releases the marbles. A counter shows how many marbles have fallen.

5. Output: a row of five result toggles, most significant bit on the left, and a readout that shows the binary and decimal value read from those toggles.

6. A DEMO button runs 5+6, then 9+7, then 15+15, resetting between runs, so it can be screen-recorded without touching anything.

7. Looks: a wooden board, brass toggles, glass marbles, warm studio lighting, soft shadows, a slow camera that follows the busiest part of the machine. It should look good in a square 1080x1080 recording.

8. Short click sounds via the Web Audio API when a toggle flips, started only after the first user click.

9. It must run at 60 fps on a normal laptop and have no console errors.

Output only the complete HTML file.
postText:
Same prompt to GPT-6 Astra and Opus 5.5, both on max: build a working computer out of marbles, in one HTML file. One prompt each, no follow-ups.

Opus 5.5: 2 h 7 min, 53.5M tokens

author: truenyl
title: Claude Opus 5.5 is absurdly good at 3D.
prompt:
Claude Opus 5.5 is absurdly good at 3D.

I reran one of my recent 3D experiments with Claude Opus 5.5.

Same prompt, same references, same real-world scene I had previously built with GPT-6 Astra.

The result was much better than I expected.

Put simply, for this specific use case, Claude Opus 5.5 was a clear win for me.

The biggest differences for me were instruction following and taste.

With the same references, Opus 5.5 got much closer to the Zelda Breath of the Wild-style look I was aiming for.

The layout felt more intentional.

It picked better camera angles.

Asset placement made more sense.

And I spent much less time fixing basic mistakes.

In my Astra version, I had to repeatedly correct things like tree roots not touching the ground, rough geometry being used where proper assets already existed, or objects being placed in ways that just looked wrong.

Opus 5.5 got much more of this right on its own.

The interesting part for me is that I have almost zero real 3D skills.

I mostly give references, look at the result, explain what feels wrong, and keep iterating.

With better instruction following and visual judgment, that loop becomes dramatically easier.

Still plenty to improve, especially indoors.

Next test is whether I can recreate the interior of the house with the same level of quality.

title: Hedgehog in the Fog Animated Short
prompt:
make an animated short that felt like Hedgehog in the Fog. I didn’t want to copy Yuri Norstein’s film, so we went with a new story.

It runs for 6.5 minutes. All 9363 frames are drawn by JavaScript code written by Opus. No video or image generation models, just canvas.

It follows a little mouse in a red scarf. Her grandfather, an old mole, is out fishing when fog rolls over the lake. She goes looking for him with a walnut-shell lantern and a sleeping firefly inside. They have a secret knock to help them find each other: short, short, long. It means "I’m here".

Norstein used paper cutouts on layers of glass, filmed frame by frame. I wanted some of that paper texture to come through in code. So the scenes use different styles: torn-paper collage, chalk on black paper, tissue paper underwater. There’s even sand on a light table and a pop-up book.

Opus wrote the music too. It found Steinway piano samples in my Logic library and used Python to compose the score around the rhythm of that knock.

I'll show this to my daughter.

It runs for 6.5 minutes. All 9363 frames are drawn by JavaScript code written by Opus. No video or image generation models, just canvas.

It follows a little mouse in a red scarf. Her grandfather, an old mole, is out fishing when fog rolls over the lake. She goes looking for him with a walnut-shell lantern and a sleeping firefly inside. They have a secret knock to help them find each other: short, short, long. It means "I’m here".

Norstein used paper cutouts on layers of glass, filmed frame by frame. I wanted some of that paper texture to come through in code. So the scenes use different styles: torn-paper collage, chalk on black paper, tissue paper underwater. There’s even sand on a light table and a pop-up book.

Opus wrote the music too. It found Steinway piano samples in my Logic library and used Python to compose the score around the rhythm of that knock.

The first version looked bad. Stiff movement, a raster pattern that hurt my eyes. I said so, and Opus reworked almost everything. The video is the result of those revisions.

Watch with sound 🔊

author: meetarno
title: X Vision Brand Promo
prompt: make a modern slick and punchy video for a modern startup that works on enabling people to grow on X, use our X Vision theme and website purpose.
postText:
Opus 5.5 is surprisingly good at motion-graphics video.

I asked it for a launch video for X Vision, our tool for growing on X. In ~3 minutes it came back with a 23-second 1080p promo. It uses our brand theme and our real logo, has product UI mockups, and comes with a soundtrack where every cut lands on the beat.

This isn't generative video. It wrote the animation in code, rendered it frame by frame and made the music itself. That means every pixel is on-brand, the text is sharp, and I can change a line and re-render in minutes.

Videos like this used to take weeks of back-and-forth with an agency and cost a lot more.

People mostly prefer watching to reading, and that changes how startups can communicate:

Marketing can ship a video for every launch and feature, not one a quarter
Sales can show how a product works in seconds instead of walking through slides
Technical teams can explain an idea with a clip instead of a long doc

And that's just inside startups.

Prompt: "make a modern slick and punchy video for a modern startup that works on enabling people to grow on X, use our X Vision theme and website purpose."

prompt:
<inputs>
Ask me for: the product name and a one-line promise, 3 to 5 UI moments to show, one accent color, 10 to 20 real vertical clips I own, and a royalty-free song with a clear drop (e.g. Mixkit, free for commercial use).
</inputs>

<direction>
High-end minimal. One idea per shot, lots of empty space, one accent color, one clean sans (Geist or Inter) with tight tracking. Masked type reveals, match cuts, one smooth camera language. Real footage only, never placeholder cards. No full stops in on-screen text.
Banned: shockwave rings, particle bursts, RGB split, camera shake, lens flares, neon glows, grid floors, flashing backgrounds, bouncy easing.
</direction>

<structure>
10 bars at 120 BPM, 2 seconds each.
Bar 1: the hook lands word by word on the beats.
Bar 2: one hook word morphs into the product UI. A cursor types and clicks.
The drop: a circle opens out of the button into a dark scene.
Then one move per bar: a wall of real clips with a scan line and 3 winners, the key output as big type, a 3D carousel of real videos with floor reflections and a motion-blurred whip onto one hero clip, the hero in a phone next to a panel that flips into results, big stats on push cuts, a 3-word ticker, a logo reveal, a fade to black.
</structure>

<build>
1. One HTML file at 1920x1080. Every style is computed from time inside 
http://
window.seek(t): no CSS animations, no timers, no state between frames.
2. Real video: extract clips to 30fps JPEG sequences with ffmpeg and swap img sources per frame. seek awaits the image decodes.
3. Analyze the song with numpy: tempo, beat grid, energy per bar, the drop. Calibrate the grid to the real kick hits. Every cut sits on a downbeat, every UI hit on a beat.
4. Render with Playwright: 3 subframes per frame at t minus, at, and plus 1/240s, then blend with ffmpeg tmix for real motion blur at 60fps.
5. Place each sound effect so its measured peak, not its file start, lands on the event. Keep the effects quiet under the music. Loudnorm to -14 LUFS.
6. Probe 20 or more frames before the full render. Fix anything cluttered, overlapping or hard to read.
</build>

<gotchas>
Never set opacity or filter on a preserve-3d element, because it flattens and both faces show. Fade its wrapper instead. Measure element positions at runtime for match cuts. Only use music and sound effects whose license allows commercial use.
</gotchas>

<start>
Ask me for the inputs, then show me a storyboard with every timing on the beat grid before you write any code.
</start>

author: majidmanzarpour
title: Create a single self-contained HTML file that renders an animated pixel ar…
prompt:
Create a single self-contained HTML file that renders an animated pixel art wizard casting a spell, using vanilla JavaScript and Canvas 2D. No external assets, libraries, or network requests.

RENDERING
- Draw everything to an offscreen canvas at a fixed logical resolution of 128x96, then blit to a fullscreen display canvas scaled by the largest integer factor that fits the window, centered, with imageSmoothingEnabled = false and CSS image-rendering: pixelated.
- All drawing snaps to integer coordinates on the logical canvas. No sub-pixel positions, anti-aliasing, gradients, or shadowBlur.
- Fixed palette of ~24 hex colors: deep blues/purples for night sky, warm robe tones, 3-4 bright magic colors. Every pixel comes from this palette.

CHARACTER
- Build the wizard procedurally from filled rects and pixel runs, ~24x32 logical pixels: pointed hat with a bend, long beard, two-shade robe with darker outline, staff with a gem at the tip.
- Parameterize the pose (staff angle, arm raise, head tilt, robe sway). Animate parameters smoothly, then quantize to the pixel grid each frame so motion reads at an 8-12 fps pixel animation feel even though the loop runs at 60fps.

ANIMATION
- Looping state machine: IDLE (2-frame bob, beard sway) -> CHARGE (staff raises, gem flickers, sparks spiral inward) -> CAST (bright burst, projectile fires across the scene, 1-2 pixel screen shake) -> RECOVER (settle back). Ease pose parameters between keyframes.
- Pooled allocation-free particle system: preallocate and reuse. Sparks orbit the gem during CHARGE, explode outward on CAST, each particle stepping its palette index from white to magic color to dark before despawn. Snap particle positions to the grid when drawing.
- Fixed 60hz timestep update with rAF rendering. Zero object allocation inside the loop.

SCENE
- Minimal background: dark sky, a few twinkling 1px stars, moon, stone floor line. Character silhouette must read clearly.
- Subtle 1px rim light on the wizard from the gem, brightening during CHARGE and CAST.

QUALITY BAR
- Crisp pixels at any window size, seamless loop, stable 60fps, readable silhouette. Should look like a polished 16-bit sprite animation, not vector shapes scaled down.
